title: Luxury Home Design in Los Angeles: The Return of Ancient Materials
subtitle: Inside Erin Foster and Simon Tikhman's AD-featured home, a quiet case for materials that age into beauty rather than date.
meta_description: What makes luxury home design in Los Angeles actually last? AD's Foster-Tikhman house shows why ancient stone and aged wood beat trend finishes every time.

faq.q: Why are LA luxury designers using ancient stone and old wood instead of new finishes?
faq.a: Because permanence reads as confidence and holds value. body_html:
Architectural Digest has published a feature on the Los Angeles home of Erin Foster and Simon Tikhman — a house the magazine describes as cozy and playful, and, more tellingly for anyone who builds here, one assembled from centuries-old woodwork and ancient stone. The AD100 designer behind it treats material as the carrier of both art and architecture, letting weathered timber and quarried stone set the emotional register of every room. The feature reads as a domestic story, but underneath it is a material argument: in a city fixated on the new, the most confident luxury now reaches for surfaces that already carry time.

Why are LA's top designers returning to ancient materials?

Because permanence has become the rarest luxury in Los Angeles. Architectural Digest reports that in the Foster-Tikhman house the AD100 designer worked with centuries-old woodwork and ancient stone rather than fabricated finishes — surfaces chosen to age into beauty instead of dating and depreciating.

The impulse is older than the trend. The materials a culture trusts to carry its most important rooms are the ones that have already outlived empires: travertine, marble, honest stone, and the quiet mass of concrete. They do not chase the eye; they reward it slowly, carrying light and wear as character rather than damage.

What does material permanence add to a luxury home?

Primarily, it protects value and feeling at once. A home built from materials that improve with age reads as confidence; one assembled from this season's finishes announces its own expiration date. Architectural Digest's framing of the Foster-Tikhman house — art and architecture held in balance by the materials themselves — is a designer's way of saying the walls will still be beautiful when the art rotates.

That matters commercially in Los Angeles, where the spec market has trained buyers to recognize — and discount — the disposable interior. Depth of material cannot be faked at the open house:

  • Stone and timber patina rather than peel, so the home looks intentional a decade on.
  • Mass materials hold light and temperature, giving rooms a stillness thin construction cannot.
  • Permanence reframes the house as an asset to keep, not a product to flip.

How does this change Los Angeles luxury design?

It shifts the conversation from style to substance. For a generation, Los Angeles luxury was measured in square footage and the newest surface. The Foster-Tikhman house, and the AD100 sensibility behind it, argue for something quieter: rooms that feel collected rather than installed, and materials that will read as deliberate a decade from now.

In a city rebuilding large parts of its housing stock, that instinct is more than taste. The homeowners now commissioning at the top of the Westside and the coast have watched trend-driven interiors age badly and resilient ones hold their value. Ancient stone and aged timber are the warm, visible end of the same logic that leads serious architecture toward concrete: choose the substance first, and let the finishes serve it. The result is a home with a longer memory — one that absorbs a family's life instead of resetting with each design cycle.

As Los Angeles rebuilds its idea of luxury, the quiet lesson of the Foster-Tikhman house will travel: the homes that feel most alive are the ones made of things that have already lasted. The next decade of design here will be measured less by what is fashionable than by what is permanent.
